doc.title: Joe Ascione interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Swinging versus timekeeping, click tracks, practicing with records
summary: He would rather swing than play metronomically. He uses click tracks for jingles and film work but not jazz, and practices with studio rather than live records.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

Is it possible to tell younger players what makes things swing?

Well I know from some teaching that I do that when I hear somebody who just has the innate quality of knowing where the pulse is, sometimes I want to say you can’t teach somebody to swing. Sometimes I say maybe you can. But I think everyone has this level of the ability to hear the full value of a quarter note let’s say. And then some of them, you know make it stretch and breathe and time does expand and contract. We’re not robots so it’s not metronomic. I’d rather swing than play steady. Dig that. Because if something’s swinging you’re tapping your foot, you’re excited, it’s feeling good. Don’t get me wrong, there’s nothing like a drummer obviously keeping time, what other function is there? But I’ve heard — I remember this one brochure I had and they asked Benny Goodman and Louis Armstrong and Doc Severinsen, all these different band leaders, what do you look for in a drummer? What do you look for? And I would say two-thirds of them would rather hear somebody swing than keep time. Some of the, obviously they say you’ve got to have a great timekeeper. Of course you do. But if you heard a guy who’s a great timekeeper but it’s not swinging, that cat’s not going to work. And if it is, I don’t want to hear that band. But if you hear a band swinging, time expands and contracts. I don’t want to say blatantly drag or rush, but it breathes. It’s got a life to it. A heartbeat to it. So I’d rather hear something that’s just swinging, the guys are playing together and everything’s resonating and it’s working and it’s swinging.
Is it hard to play with a click track because of that, time expanding and—

Well I’ll use a click track on a jingle, a movie thing, a contemporary setting, even a book, an instructional book project. So those type of things I’ll use a click track. No I don’t have a problem. I don’t have a problem doing that. In fact I like it. It’s kind of fun. It’s easier than playing tennis. But for jazz, I don’t really care to use it.
No, I just wondered, you know because you were saying that the time can move a bit.

I’ll never practice — when I was a kid I had a teacher who said he went to I think Ithaca College perhaps. Greg Prios. Great teacher. Great musician, great teacher. And he said to me, “If you’re practicing with records, don’t use live recordings. More often than not the time is moving around more than you’d care to hear.” And I stuck with that and it’s sort of true.
